issues.legal_issue: A decree in a separate proceeding concerning a third party’s title does not provide a fresh starting point for limitation when it leaves the decree sought to be executed unchanged.
material_facts: The decree-holder sought to execute a foreclosure decree against the judgment debtor.
In a separate suit, the judgment debtor’s son obtained a declaration that the foreclosure decree did not bind him as to his half share and an injunction preventing execution against that share.
The separate proceeding did not reverse, vary, or amend the foreclosure decree as it applied to the judgment debtor.
issues.conclusion: The separate suit’s appellate decree did not provide a fresh starting point for limitation under clauses 1, 2, or 4 of Article 182.
issues.legal_principle: Under clauses 1, 2, and 4 of Article 182 of the Limitation Act 1908, a fresh starting point arises from the decree being executed, an appeal concerning that decree, or an amendment of that decree. A decision in a collateral proceeding that leaves the decree unchanged does not qualify. The Court relied on Bhawanipore Banking Corporation Ltd. v. Gori Shanker Sharma.

predicates.execution_limitation_case: A decree-holder applies to execute a decree and limitation is disputed.
predicates.separate_proceeding_concerns_third_party: A separate proceeding determines a third party’s rights in property covered by the decree.
predicates.original_execution_decree_unchanged: The separate proceeding does not reverse, vary, or amend the decree as it applies to the judgment debtor.

issues.definition: When execution limitation is disputed, a separate proceeding about a third party’s title does not restart limitation if it leaves the execution decree unchanged as against the judgment debtor.

issues.legal_issue: A defensive written statement that makes no request to the court is not an application for a step in aid of execution, and an appeal to a court that is not the proper executing court does not establish the required application to that court.
material_facts: The decree-holder filed a written statement opposing a suit brought by the judgment debtor’s son, seeking to prevent execution of the foreclosure decree.
The decree-holder later appealed in the High Court against the decision in that separate litigation.
The High Court was not the court whose duty it was to execute the foreclosure decree.
The Supreme Court did not decide whether the written statement, resistance to the appeal, or the second appeal otherwise amounted to a step in aid of execution.
issues.conclusion: The decree-holder could not obtain a fresh starting point under clause 5 of Article 182 because the written statement was not an application and the High Court appeal was not an application to the proper court. Justice Goswami dissented, concluding that the defensive steps in the related litigation were steps in aid of execution.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 5 of Article 182 of the Limitation Act 1908 requires a lawful application to the proper court to take a step in aid of execution. Explanation II defines the proper court by reference to the court whose duty it is to execute the decree; section 38 of the Code of Civil Procedure identifies the court that passed the decree or a court to which it is sent for execution. A written statement ordinarily makes no request to the court and is simply a defence, unlike a request or petition. The Court relied on V.E.A. Annamalai Chettiar v. Valliammai Achi, and distinguished Panna Lal v. Smt. Saraswati Devi and Kartar Singh v. Sultan Singh Partap Singh.

predicates.execution_limitation_case: A decree-holder applies to execute a decree and limitation is disputed.
predicates.defensive_pleading_makes_no_request: The decree-holder files a pleading only to defend against another party’s claim and does not request relief from the court.
predicates.appeal_court_not_proper_executing_court: The decree-holder appeals in a court that is not responsible for executing the decree.

issues.definition: In an execution limitation case, a purely defensive pleading and an appeal to a court that does not execute the decree do not restart limitation under the step-in-aid rule.

issues.legal_issue: A later execution application is not a continuation or revival of an earlier application that was finally dismissed because the decree-holder failed to take a required step.
material_facts: The earlier execution application was dismissed after the decree-holder failed to pay the process fee required for a warrant of possession.
The earlier application was not left pending.
The decree-holder later filed another application seeking possession.
issues.conclusion: The later application was not a continuation or revival of the earlier application.
issues.legal_principle: A later execution application may be treated as a continuation or revival only where the earlier application remains pending or was dismissed through no fault of the decree-holder, and the applications are substantially similar in scope and character. A properly and finally disposed-of application cannot be revived by a later application. The Court relied on Vadlamannati Bala Tripura Sundaramma v. Abdul Khader.

predicates.execution_limitation_case: A decree-holder applies to execute a decree and limitation is disputed.
predicates.prior_application_finally_dismissed_for_: An earlier execution application was finally dismissed because the decree-holder failed to take a required procedural step.
predicates.prior_application_not_pending: The earlier execution application was no longer pending when the later application was filed.

issues.definition: A later execution application is not a revival when the earlier application was finally dismissed for the decree-holder’s default and was no longer pending.
